note: Two halves of one state song culture. Shōka: Ministry of Education school songs from the 1884 songbook (Aogeba tōtoshi) through the Monbushō shōka of 1910–14 (Furusato, Haru no ogawa, Oborozukiyo) and the middle-school songs of Taki Rentarō (Kōjō no tsuki, Hakone hachiri), in later choir recordings. Gunka: from the first composed military song (Battōtai, 1885) and the Sino- and Russo-Japanese war songs, in Columbia's later recordings, to original 78s of the 1937–43 record-company hits (Roei no uta, Aikoku kōshinkyoku, Wakawashi no uta). Release years are null where the only date is a compilation's.

size.basis: No source counts recordings; a judgement. The repertoire is large: Japanese Wikipedia says 1,300 gunka and 140 gunka songbooks were made in the two years of the Sino-Japanese War alone, the 1881-84 school songbook held 91 songs and the 1911-14 Jinjō shōgaku shōka 120, and Tetsudō shōka alone runs to 334 verses in five volumes. From 1931 the record companies mass-produced gunka on 78s (one Columbia reissue of original 78s holds 73 tracks), and after the 1952 end of the ban every major label issued multi-volume gunka sets (Columbia, King, Teichiku, Victor, Pony Canyon seen on iTunes Japan) while choirs and singers keep re-recording the school songs. Most songs exist in several recordings. An insider's essential list is about 50 songs, half school songs, half military.
